column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check

The article does not mention Upper Creek towns as such; it says the Creek held the lower valley and the Cherokee the upper after the Revolutionary War. De Soto's year (1540) left out of the text only to avoid repeating the description.
Heading 'Organisation and way of life' used for the composition of the assembly (institution).

The article spells the city Malmø and the checker accepts only that form; the entry has Malmö. The entry calls Christopher's opponent the Lutheran Duke Christian of Holstein; the article says Duke Christian of Gottorp, used here without contradiction.

The entry calls Dagobert the first Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem; the article calls him the second, elected after Arnulf of Chocques was deposed as patriarch. Arnulf's earlier patriarchate is therefore left out of the text.
The article gives the helmet's date as probably the 3rd century BCE; not used. 'Is currently placed on the UNESCO Tentative list' rendered without 'currently'.
The article calls the founder Ernest Ludwig / Ernst Ludwig; the entry's 'Ernest Louis' is kept.
The entry says Toro was overthrown by Germán Busch; the article says he resigned and Busch assumed the presidency (a soft coup). Worded as a resignation, which does not contradict the entry.

Short article (about 430 words); two sections, keeping to Herodotus's account as the article gives it. The article both says Atossa's cure won him leave to visit Greece and that he went west in Persian custody; both kept, attributed to Herodotus.

The article gives his death as late March 264 and his birth as c. 197; the entry's 197–264 is not contradicted. The article is given as lead and section openings; the route detail via Deyang and Fu County comes from Deng Ai's proposal as quoted.

Short article (about 330 words); two sections. The article describes Dinguiraye as the first capital of the Tukulor Empire and the town as in 'northern Guinea' (the entry says north-eastern); the direction is kept as 'northern', which does not contradict. The article says the mosque 'until recently was thatched'; worded as 'long covered with a thatched roof' without dating the change.

The entry says he resisted in 1888, was exiled and returned in 1898; the article says he was captured in 1890, exiled for seven years and released when Zululand was incorporated into Natal in 1897, installed as induna the following year. Years of exile and release left out. Article gives birth as c. 1868.

The article gives his birth as 1323; the entry has 1322. Birth year left out. The article spells the daughter Eudoxia, the entry Evdokia; she is left unnamed. Short article (about 330 words); written close to its substance.
The article mentions that other sources give his birth as 1271; the entry's 1275 is the more accepted tradition and is not contradicted (birth year not printed).

The article gives the war's end as 24 January 1856 in its lead but dates the Battle of Sabana Larga to 27 January 1856; the exact end date and the battle's day are left out. Duarte, Mella and Sánchez are named in the entry with full names.
The article dates the Wei invasion and sack of Hwando to 244; the entry gives 244–245, so the year of the sack is left out. Birth year 209 from the article not used.
Present-day Brazilian politicians of the Costa Doria family left out. The article names several Doria admirals; the 1284 and 1298 dates are in the entry and not repeated.

Short article (about 450 words). The article says Washington accepted and used the doctrine, and also that the Roosevelt Corollary was issued in response to it; both reflected without judging between them.

The entry dates the founding by tradition to around 1346–1347 and Bogdan's expulsion of Dragoș's heirs to around 1359; the article says most chronicles put Dragoș's arrival in 1359 (others 1352, 1347 or 1345) and his death traditionally in 1361 (others 1353, c. 1354, 1357). All years of arrival, death and the expulsion are left out of the text.

The entry places the murder in a church at Montolio; the article says the chapel of his castle at Monte Ilario, near Bovino. The place name is left out. The entry speaks of a probable conspiracy of Lombard nobles; the article says he was possibly the victim of an anti-Norman conspiracy led by Argyrus, the Byzantine catepan. The conspiracy's leader is left out; only Malaterra's Lombard killer is given.
Duleek railway station (1850-1958) and modern notable people left out as not historical substance.

The article says the dynasty ruled Vengi until c. 1001 CE and lists rulers to 1102; the entry gives 624-c. 1070. The end date is left out. The article gives 848 for Gunaga Vijayaditya III's accession in one place and 849 in the ruler list; no year printed.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance; beyond the entry it gives only his parents, the dates of his joint rule of Montbéliard and the names of his children

The article gives his death as 16 December 867 and dates the will 867; the entry gives c. 815-866. Neither the death year nor the will's year is printed. The article's claim that he drove the Bulgars from Italy in 825-830 (when he would have been about ten) is left out as doubtful. The article's 'Character' section is hagiographic and unsourced; not used.
Used 22 November 643 from the article; the entry says November 643, consistent.

Left out as assessments of the present government: the claim that the orchestra is perceived as a propaganda instrument, and the Maduro administration as its most generous patron. The article says the bank studied 'more than 2,000,000 young people' educated in El Sistema, against 700,000 musicians in 2015; not used.
The article places Isny in Bavaria; the place name alone is used. The line about a living descendant (David Cameron) is left out.
The article and the entry agree on 1368, 1382, about 500 and 14,000 members, Lan Yu (1393) and 1644; these are not repeated.
The lead says the Northern Song capital was captured in 1127; the body places the second siege from August 1126. No year given for the fall itself, beyond the entry's own.

Short article; the text uses nearly all of it. The article says Erchanger was duke from September 915; the entry says he defeated the king's supporters at Wahlwies in 915. The article does not say Berthold was executed with him (the entry does); not repeated or contradicted. The article says 'executed on the instructions of the king'; the entry says Conrad had him executed. Consistent.

The article dates the poem between 1590 and 1610 from the poet's dates; the entry says early 17th century. The dating is left out. The article calls him Vikentios Kornaros in its lead and Vitsentzos Kornaros later; the latter is used, as in the entry.

The article says it first appeared in print in 1599 in Cologne and calls the book both the Speyer Hymnbook and the Speyer Hymnal (printed in Cologne); written as one book. The tune is also used for A Great and Mighty Wonder, which the article attributes to Germanus of Auxerre; left out as doubtful.
The article does not mention Cetshwayo's death at Eshowe in 1884 (in the entry); not repeated. The article says 'relieved on April 3'; written day-first as 3 April (1879).
The entry calls the Pillar of the Boatmen a 1st-century monument; the article dates it to Tiberius (14-37 CE), consistent.

The article says in one place he died sometime after 618 and in another that his name is not attested after 613; no death date given. The article spells the name Ŭlchi Mundŏk (McCune-Reischauer); the text avoids the entry's spelling Eulji Mundeok, which the checker does not find in the article, and uses the article's form only for the title element and the poem.
Short article; text uses nearly all of it.

The article gives several dates for his grant of Caesarea (1101 in the lead and in Moeller, around 1108 in Ringel, before September 1110 in the body); the entry says about the same time as Sidon (1110). No year printed for Caesarea. The article's lead calls him lord of Sidon in 1110; consistent with the entry.
Short article; text kept to what it gives. No conflict with the entry.

The article says the first baptisms were on 21 January 1525 at Manz's house (entry: January 1525, consistent). It says he was drowned 'in Lake Zürich on the Limmat'; the entry says the Limmat, so the place of drowning is not repeated.

The article says the Imperial ban was imposed in 1701 by Leopold I and confirmed by the Diet on 30 June 1708; its lead says he was dispossessed by an Imperial ban in 1708. Only the 1708 confirmation is given. The article also says the coalition conquered Mantua in 1701 and that he left Anna Isabella as regent; left out as doubtful. Charleville (in the entry) is not in the article.
The article gives Hassig without a first name. The article spells the conquistador's name 'Cortez', kept so here.

The article says the road was built during the first and second centuries; the entry dates it to the 1st century and says it was built in the first decades after 43 CE. The second century is left out. The article does not give the 370 km total length.
The article dates the conquest of Rhodes to 1308 and 1309; the entry says it began in 1306 and the city fell around 1309-1310. The dates of the conquest are left out.

The article's lead gives c. 1479 but its body says he was born about 1473; the entry has c. 1479, so no birth year is given. The article says the fleet sailed from Seville at the end of June 1526, before the petition of 19 November 1526 was approved; the entry says the campaigns began in 1527. The sailing year is left out.
No conflict with the entry found.

The article says he travelled to Brazil in 1636 and lived there from 1637 to 1644, and elsewhere that he returned in 1642; the entry has 1637 to 1644. The year of his return is not given. The article says 1669 is both the date of his last letter and the year he stopped painting Brazilian scenes.
The list of abbesses in the article gives Hildegard's dates as 828-856 or 859, before the foundation of 853; no dates for her are given.
SKIPPED: The article has under 250 words of substance beyond the entry: a few lines on his appanage and a list of his children and their marriages.
No conflict with the entry found.

The article dates his death to 16 October 385 and says the strangling was in fall 385; consistent with the entry. The article's list of rulers conquered includes Chouchi as well as those in the entry.
Short article, mostly a list of offices and children; written in two sections.

The article says the accusation came shortly after Ieyasu's death in 1619; the entry dates the loss of the domain to 1619. Ieyasu's death is not dated here. The article mixes calendars in its dates of the 1600 campaign (21 and 22 August, 29 September, 21 October), so no day dates are given for it.

The article says city status was granted by Abdulla Yameen's decree of 4 June 2017, and elsewhere that the government recognised the island as a city in 2016; no year is given. The article's sections are only partly given (lead and openings).
Short article; two sections.

The entry calls her son Ramon Berenguer IV; the article calls him Raymond Berengar V. The son is not named here. The article gives her death as c. 1242/1257 and says she may have been alive in 1257; the entry has c. 1242, so the 1257 donation is left out.
No conflict with the entry found.

The article says Gobir was founded in the 12th century and elsewhere that it traced a lineage to the 11th century; no founding date is given. The 2024 abduction and murder of a traditional ruler is left out as not about the historical kingdom.

The article says the tradition of unmarried royal daughters adopting their successors was inaugurated by Ramesses VI in the Twentieth Dynasty; the entry places it from the Third Intermediate Period. The start of that custom is left out.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance (course, two dams, crops) and adds little beyond the description; its pollution paragraph is speculation about a future oil find
The article gives 137 volumes; the entry says 139. The number of volumes is left out.

The article dates the famine 1848-1850 with the fall from 89,000 to 9,000; the entry dates it 1849-1850. The text gives only the population figures for 1848 and 1850, not the famine's start. The article says Grobogan 'became the center of the Mataram kingdom'; worded as local tradition since it rests on the folk capital Medhang Kamulan.
The entry names the Six Articles; the article speaks only of the order of 28 June 1832 tightening the Carlsbad Decrees, so the text uses that wording.
The article has the temple destroyed in 1779 as well as in 1828; the entry names only the 1828 destruction. Both are consistent; the text tells both.

The entry says the Hittites came to identify her with the sun goddess of Arinna; the article stresses the equation had limited recognition. The text states the prayer and attributes the doubt to Taracha, without denying the identification.
The article names Schmerling only by surname, so the text does too.

The History of the Britons dates Vortigern's welcome to 447, the Chronicle to 449, which the entry gives. The text gives no year for the arrival. The entry says the brothers led Jutes; the article says Angles, Saxons and Jutes. The text does not name their people.
The article names Fox only by surname, so the text does too.
The article names Reid only by surname, so the text does too.
The Treaty of Riechenberg named in the entry is not in the article.

The article gives the 1913 fraud sentence as two years in one place and, quoting Dele-Cole, five years in another; the text gives no length. The 2025 posthumous pardon by President Bola Tinubu is left out (present-day act of a sitting government); the editor may add it as a bare dated fact.
The article gives the length as 7,028 to 7,760 metres in one place and 7.5 km in another; the text uses 7.5 km.

The article gives his birth as c. 1729 and 1729; the entry's dates are 1728-1780. The birth year is left out. The article's lead says he died 1779 or 1780; its narrative has him die on 24 January after an arrest in late 1779, which agrees with the entry's 1780.
The article says Ujimasa retired in 1590 and Ujinao became head of the clan; it also has him lead the defence of Odawara. The 1590 retirement is left out.

The article's sentence on Sigismund's invasion is garbled ('would leave Bosnia alone since 1389, and the same year King Sigismund invaded'); the year of that invasion is left out. The Latin coin legend is rendered in English.

The article dates the entry into the subcontinent to the end of the 5th or early 6th century, but also records Skandagupta repulsing an attack in 460; the entry's 'from the mid-fifth century' is not restated. The article is short, so the text is near the lower limit.

The article dates the tropical wave's departure from Africa to 25 June in the lead and 23 June in its meteorological history; no date given. Its tornado totals also differ (68 + 2 in the lead, 71 later); left out. The Union Island percentages differ (80-90% damaged vs over 90% damaged or destroyed) and are left out. The entry gives about 240 km/h at the Grenadines landfall; the article gives 270 km/h only for the peak the next morning, which is what is printed.

The article says he left Algiers on 15 July 1830, 'five days after his surrender', but also that the French entered Algiers on 5 July; the 'five days' is left out. The article gives the birth year as 1765 without 'c.'; the entry's dates are not restated.
The excerpt does not describe the Battle of Dayr al-Jamajim itself beyond the lead; it is not restated. Al-Tabari's account is named for the early episodes.

The entry says the tablets were found at Gubbio; the article gives two versions, a field near Scheggia (which it prefers) and the Roman theatre in Gubbio. The place of the find is left out. The article spells the editor both Kirkhoff and Kirchhoff.

The article gives his ages inconsistently (18 both at the Tanaka castle attack and in 1578); ages are left out. Its family section calls his first son Naokatsu, the death section Naotsugu; the death section's name is used.

The article says about 199 settlements would be fully or partly affected, against the entry's 'dozens of villages'; the figure is left out. The article's design and output figures are partly in the future tense ('will support'); only the plant's capacity and the reservoir's capacity are given.
The entry dates the new charter to 1691; the article calls it the 1692 charter. No year is given for it here. The article's dates are Old Style; they are printed as it gives them.

The article attributes the name Duchy of Inflanty to a 1667 bill in one place and to the Warsaw Sejm of 1677 in another; the duchy title is left out. It names five seats for 'four' tracts; the tracts are left out. The voivodes' list runs past the 1772 partition (titular office); not used.

SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance; it adds only a few measurements and the ruin dates to the entry. It also names the architect as 'Ali b. Mushaimish al-Dimashqi, differing from the entry's Ali ibn al-Dimishqi.

The article dates the pope's approval of the Treaty of Granada to 25 June 1500, before the treaty's own date of 11 November 1500; left out. It calls the Neapolitan king both Frederick and Frederick IV; 'Frederick of Naples' is used.

The article gives two origins (descendants of the Chanes of Tabasco; possibly from Motul de San José) and both are given as differing accounts. It dates Cortés's expedition and visit to Nojpetén to 1523; no year is given here. Its speaker counts are inconsistent (1,094 in the 2002 census, 36 now, 12 fluent in 1986); only the 36 of the lead is used. The 230,000 square kilometre 'empire' and the Malintzin story are left out as doubtful.

The article's sentence on the lieutenancy ('Isabella, daughter of Peter IV of Aragon, who appointed him lieutenant ... in 1408') is ambiguous, since Peter IV was long dead; the appointer is not named. The article is short and the text is near the lower limit.
The entry gives his term as Political Agent as 1818-1822; the article says he resigned in 1823. The year of resignation is left out.
The article is short (about 370 words); the text stays near the lower limit.
The article's 'Thermoplylae' (a slip) is not used. Whether Jason aimed to rule all Greece is left as the article leaves it, speculation.

The entry says the city was abandoned in the 14th century; the article says it was abandoned after its destruction by the Mongols under Genghis Khan in the 13th century. The abandonment is left out. The article's 'From 450 AD until 640 AD it became Jiao prefecture in the Tang dynasty' is anachronistic and left out.

The entry dates Ran Min's massacre to 350; the article places the killing order 'by the end of the year' 349, gives 349-350 in its lead, and has Shi Min take the name Ran Min in 350. No year is given here for the massacre. The Legacy paragraph is short (about 45 words).
The article is mostly a list of commands; the text draws on its lead and the dated entries. An Lushan's army is given as '150 000' in the article; written 'a large army'.
Article gives Schaffhausen as birthplace; the entry says he was raised in Kaysersberg, which agrees.

The article says he inherited the duchy on Wilhelm August's death in 1671 and was confirmed in Eisenach by the 1672 division; the entry says he received Eisenach as a separate duchy in 1672. The year 1671 is left out to avoid a clash.
Short article, mostly a list of children; text kept near the lower limit. The entry's points on Sponheim and the Electoral Palatinate are not in the article and are not repeated.

The entry says he spent some seventeen years in Constantinople; the article says seven years, while also giving Collins's dates c. 562-c. 579 (about seventeen years) and Wolf's c. 569-c. 576 (seven). The length of stay is not stated; only the two scholars' dates are given. The article dates the chronicle 568-590 in the lead but gives 567 as John's point of departure; the entry says 567 to 590. The starting year is not printed.
The lead says the Treaty Party treaty required removal by 1838; consistent with the entry.

The article says the succession dispute became part of the Thirty Years' War; the entry says it threatened a European war before the duchies were partitioned. The relation between the two wars is left vague to avoid a clash.
The article dates the Battle of Pasto 10 May 1813, before the other battles of 1813-1814; the dates of the battles are left out.

The entry says he withdrew Guatemala from the Federation of Central America; the article says he encouraged an unsuccessful tripartite republic with Honduras and El Salvador and that Congress ratified the Central American Union Covenant. The federation is left out of the text.

The entry calls Salcedo Legazpi's grandson; the article's lead says nephew, though some records say grandson, and its personal life section makes his mother Legazpi's daughter. The relationship is left out. The article dates the Manila campaign to 1567, when Salcedo was 18; the year is left out. The romance with Kandarapa is told at length in the article from Cepeda's account; mentioned only briefly as an account.
The article's account of 1954 is written in a partisan tone ('our 39th President'); only its facts are used.
The essayist is spelled without accents, as in the source: Jose Maria Gutierrez Estrada.

Article says Ottoman historian Saadeddin Efendi placed his death in the Harput Mountains; Schiltberger and Ibn Arabshah give Dhu al-Qa'da (July-August) 1398. Only the year is used, as in the entry. Article states his death site as the Karabel region; left out. Entry's 'Turkmen tribes' and 'held off for nearly two decades' agree with the article's 17-18 years of rule.
The entry calls the mine the first successful metal mine in Australia; the article does not say so, and it is not repeated.

The article says the Shilaharas of Kolhapur ruled Satara and Belagavi districts from 1000 to 1215; the entry says they arose in the region in the 10th century. The dates are left out. The article lists the mosque among places 2 km from Karad; 'near the town' is used.

The article calls Karamchand's father Uttamchand in one paragraph and Ananyachand in another; Uttamchand agrees with the entry and is used. The entry mentions Vankaner; the article does not, and it is not repeated.
The article gives 20 May 1820 as his death date in the lead and 5 May 1820 as the sentence; consistent.
Spelling follows the article (Kaštiliašu); the entry's title is Kashtiliash IV.
SKIPPED: article under 300 words, little beyond the existing description

The entry says the Khasa Malla kingdom ruled from Sinja near Jumla; the article says it ruled Humla from the eleventh century. Where it ruled is left out. The article gives two dates for the arrival of the Khas in western Nepal (early first millennium BCE or mid first millennium CE); left out.
The entry says the shale was carved into furniture; the article does not mention furniture and it is not repeated. The article's current yield of the oil well is left out (present-day figure).
The article gives her death as 2 July 1706; the entry has 1706 only, consistent. The article spells the priest both 'Bernardo de Gallo' and 'Bernardo da Gallo'; I used 'da Gallo'.
The article mentions the Strategies of the Warring States alongside the Records of the Grand Historian as sources for his continued standing; I named only the latter for length.

Short article with much of it a list of villages; text kept near the lower limit. The article says the river empties into the Main 'after about 82 kilometres' but also gives its length as 87 km; I used 87 only.

The entry calls the Tassilo Chalice gilded copper given by Tassilo and his wife Liutpirga; the article gives it as copper and silver-gilt, donated by Tassilo III, and does not name Liutpirga. I left the chalice out. The art-storage letter named Hans Posse and Martin Bormann; I kept it general.

The entry dates his rule from 1894; the article says he ascended the throne on 1 February 1895 after his father's death on 28 December 1894, with his mother regent 1895-1902. I left out the accession date and the regency years. The article gives both 8 February and 8 August 1902 for his taking over; I gave the year only.
The article says the pardon by John J. McCloy restored Krupp's holdings; I gave only the release date. Big Bertha date as the article: 1914.
The article names Olga Arjanne as his wife from 1908 and later Hanna Malm as his wife; I mentioned only Malm.
The 2011 figures: 36.37% Hinduism, 30.24% Christianity, 29.2% Sarna; rounded.

The article calls the opera's role in the Belgian Revolution 'alleged' and suggests the rebels had fixed the date beforehand, so its role may have been a marriage of convenience; the entry says the performance sparked the riots. I gave the posters as fact without the judgement. Accounts differ on when in the opera the exodus began; I did not name the moment beyond the duet.

The entry dates the Landtag to 1933 and says the Nazis dissolved it then; the article says the Law on the Reconstruction of the Reich abolished it with effect from 30 January 1934 (its last meeting was 18 May 1933). I left out the abolition date. The entry calls the post-1918 Landtag a single chamber; the article says the Prussian State Council succeeded the Herrenhaus as a kind of upper house. I left the State Council out.

The article dates Mithridates VI's return to 116-113 BCE and her regency to 120-116 (perhaps up to 113), and her death to 115-113; the entry has c. 113. I gave no dates for his return or her death. The article says she died in prison of natural causes; the entry says 'is thought to have died in prison', consistent.

The entry says the site was abandoned around 700 BCE; the article says occupation ended at the beginning of the Archaic period (early 7th century BCE). I gave no date for the end. The article says excavation was 'ongoing as of 2015'; I gave only the earlier campaigns.
The article names two men called Wang Zun: the governor of 30 CE and a Lelang leader who joined Murong Hui in the Jin period; I named only the first.

The article calls him the last ruler of the Despotate of Epirus; the entry calls him titular despot and last ruler of the County Palatine of Cephalonia and Zakynthos. I avoided either characterisation. The article gives his death as before August 1503; the entry 'd. 1503', consistent; I gave no year.

The entry calls his rival Zhu Wen; the article uses only the name Zhu Quanzhong. The article does not say Li Keyong's forces drove Huang Chao from Chang'an in 883 (the entry's claim); it is a lead-and-section excerpt and the section on the recapture is not given, so I did not mention it either way.

The entry dates the Xiongnu victory to the 240s BCE; the article gives no date for it (only that he was stationed in Yanmen from 265 BCE). I gave no date for the victory. The entry says he was executed; the article says he was either executed or forced to commit suicide; I wrote only that he died on the king's orders.

The article gives the party 62 of 128 seats in 2005 and, in the 2009 section, says it dropped to 45 'from its previous 61'; I gave only the 45. I left out the article's present-day description of the party as centre-right and its stance on abortion. The article does not name Policarpo Bonilla.

The entry's description says the Red Army took Vilnius as it advanced in December 1918; the article dates the capture to 5 January 1919 after a five-day fight with Polish paramilitary units. The text does not date the capture. Article lead says Lithuanian army began its offensive in mid-May; body says first operation 18 May after capturing Ukmergė on 3 May. Kept to 'from May'.

SKIPPED: The article has under 250 words of substance: a short history already in the entry, census figures given 'as of' 2023, constituencies and a list of notable people. The article adds that a Central Dir District was carved out of Lower and Upper Dir on 22 January 2023; not used.

Article gives his death as c. 1383 (lead) and c. 1385 (body); the entry has d. c. 1384. Death year left out. Article says he ruled Volhynia 'for roughly sixty years' and from 1320; the entry says he became ruler of Volhynia after 1340. Left out. Article says in 1370 he 'captured all of Volhynia'; the entry says he kept 'most of Volhynia'. Worded as winning back Volhynian lands.

Article lead says the dynasty ruled Bavaria 'in the ninth century'; the entry says late ninth and tenth centuries. Not stated. Article says Luitpold 'was killed in the 907 Battle of Pressburg' — already in the entry; not repeated.
Article writes 177 BC (BCE).
Article has little beyond this; nothing of Mago's life is known, so the text covers the work and its translations only. Article dates the destruction to 146 BC, as the entry does.
The article's 'Malaysia's best-selling English newspaper' claim about The Star omitted (ranking). Henry H.S. Lee named as Malaysia's first finance minister in the article; not used.

The article numbers the last head both Mushegh IV (+772) and Mushegh VI (killed at Bagrevand, mid-770s); the number is left out. The article dates the final revolt 774/75 and 774–775; the entry says only 'the 8th century'.

Article: 'fl. 1031–1040'; date of death unknown. The entry's 'd. c. 1040' is not contradicted: the text says only that no poem seems to postdate his time at the court of Ghazna. The article writes the sultan's name with diacritics (Masʿūd) and 'Ghaznawid'; to avoid spellings different from the entry's (Mas'ud, Ghaznavid), the text says 'the sultan' after the entry's own naming.
Article lead dates the conquest of Tabaristan to 932; the body tells of an attack after Makan's return from Nishapur in 931. The entry says around 930. The text does not date it.
Article spells 'Seventh-Day Adventists'.

The article dates the Great Chicago Fire to 1880 (it was in 1871, her birth year); the year is left out. The entry dates the Canberra competition win to 1912; the article gives no year, so none is given here. The article says she worked for Wright for 'fifteen years' but also 1895–1909; the figure is left out.
The article gives his birth as 12 September 1759 (lead) and 10 September 1759 (same paragraph); the day is left out.

The article gives the heart's later excavation as 1998 (lead) and 1996 (body); only the 1998 reburial date, given once, is used. The article says the rebuilding after 1385 took about 100 years and was unfinished when James IV visited in 1504; the entry says it was largely rebuilt in the late 14th century. The length of the rebuilding is left out. Article says the Cistercians founded it 'at the request of' David I; the entry says founded by David I. Not contradicted.

The article places the defeat at Cannae in October 1017 (the 'stunning reverse' in October after the gains of May to September 1017); the entry dates the battle at Cannae to 1018. The text does not date the battle. The article writes 216 BC (BCE).
The article writes 48 BC (BCE).

Article says they assimilated 'around the 16th century'; the entry says Ryazan, Moscow and the Qasim Khanate absorbed them. Not contradicted. Article spells the monastery's village Radovitsy and Radovitsky; Radovitsy used.

Article: died c. 1390; entry: after 1390. Death not stated. Article spells 'Spyrindon P. Lambros'; the first name is left out. Article says both 'at least five entries ... 1395 to 1426 (or 1429)' by continuators and 'the last four entries'; the number is left out.

The article gives the end of the Mihna as banned around 851 and abolished 'between 848 and 851', and its length as eighteen years and 'about fifteen years'. These figures are left out; the entry's 847 and c. 851 are not restated. The article spells Ibn Abi Du'ad also as Ibn Abi Duwad and Ahmed ibn Hanbal; the entry's Ahmad ibn Hanbal used.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance and adds little to the entry; it also gives the chronicle as covering 1594-1660 where the entry has 1595-1661
